title: The Korean War Explained in 9 Minutes
summary:
In 1945, two young American colonels got about thirty minutes to split Korea in half. Five years later North Korea invaded across that line, the United States and the United Nations jumped in, and China followed. Seoul changed hands four times in nine months, and by 1953 the border was back almost exactly where the pencil line had been.

This map-based explainer walks through the Korean War step by step: the 38th parallel, the Pusan Perimeter, the Inchon landing, the Chosin Reservoir, MacArthur's firing, two years of truce talks, and what the war cost. #KoreanWar #History #Maps
sources: Wikipedia, Korean War, Division of Korea, Battle of Osan, Pusan Perimeter, Battle of Inchon, Chinese intervention in the Korean War, Battle of Chosin Reservoir, Hungnam evacuation, Korean Armistice Agreement, Korean Demilitarized Zone (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War and related articles; used as a cross-check of dates and numbers, checked 2026-11-17)

Further reading (not consulted for the 2026-11-17 check): Allan R. Millett, The War for Korea, 1945-1950 and 1950-1951 (University Press of Kansas); David Halberstam, The Coldest Winter (Hyperion, 2007); Max Hastings, The Korean War (Simon & Schuster, 1987); Bruce Cumings, The Korean War: A History (Modern Library, 2010); U.S. Army Center of Military History, The United States Army in the Korean War series (history.army.mil)
caveats: Casualty figures are estimates. U.S. dead (36,574 in the Korean theater) is the Defense Department count; South Korea's military dead (137,899) is the South Korean defense ministry figure; Chinese (about 183,000 to 198,000) and North Korean (about 294,000 to 317,000) military dead are low-end published estimates and are disputed.
Civilian death estimates range widely, from about 1.5 million to 3 million.

Some counts and dates differ between sources: North Korea's T-34 tanks at the start of the invasion (about 120 to 150), the exact night of the 38th parallel decision (August 10 to 11, from Dean Rusk's memory), and the day Seoul was retaken in March 1951 (March 14 to 15).

Maps are simplified and redrawn for this video; borders, front lines and the Pusan Perimeter are approximate (roughly 15 to 30 miles), and the territory colors change in large blocks rather than along the exact front line.

review.angle: Cold open: two officers, thirty minutes, one line that barely moved in three years. The line returns in chapter 9.

shorts.title: A 30-Foot Tide and One Risky Plan

shorts.title: 30 Minutes to Split a Country

shorts.hook: How do you fight at 30 below zero?
shorts.title: Surrounded at 30 Below Zero

beats.say: Two American officers drew the line that split Korea in about half an hour. Then the whole world fought over it for three years, and the line barely moved.
That's the Korean War. It pulled in the United States, China, and more than a dozen other countries. And it never officially ended.
The whole peninsula is about the size of Utah. Let's see how a place that small ended up dragging in the whole world.
Korea had been ruled by Japan for 35 years. When Japan lost World War Two in August 1945, someone had to take its surrender there.
Soviet troops were already pushing in from the north. The nearest American troops were hundreds of miles away.
So on the night of August 10, two young colonels got about thirty minutes to find a dividing line. One of them was Dean Rusk, who later became Secretary of State.

do.ask: Where do you cut a country?

beats.say: They had no time to study the land. They picked the 38th parallel, a straight line across the middle. It kept the capital, Seoul, on the American side.
It was quick, and it was simple. And nobody asked a single Korean.
The Soviets agreed to the line. Over the next three years, the two halves grew apart, and each government said it ruled the whole country.
Before dawn on Sunday, June 25, 1950, North Korean guns opened up along the 38th parallel. Then the tanks rolled south. Many South Korean soldiers were home on weekend leave.
Around 120 Soviet-built T-34 tanks led the way. South Korea had no tanks of its own.
Seoul sits only about 30 miles from the border, like Dallas to Fort Worth. It fell in three days.
The United Nations Security Council told North Korea to stop. The Soviet Union could have vetoed that. But it was boycotting the council, so nobody was in the chair.
Truman called it a police action, and Congress never declared war. That's one reason it's often called the Forgotten War.
The first Americans to fight were a small group called Task Force Smith. About 540 soldiers dug in near Osan on July 5 and tried to stop a column of tanks. Many of them had never been in a fight.
Their shells barely scratched the tanks. They held for a few hours and then had to run. The North Koreans kept rolling south.
By early August, UN forces were crammed into a corner of the southeast, with the sea at their backs. It was called the Pusan Perimeter.
The U.S. Eighth Army commander, General Walton Walker, ordered his men to stand and fight. Reserves raced from one weak spot to another by truck and train.
For six weeks, they held a box in the corner of Korea, with the Nakdong River in front and the sea behind. If they lost, the war was over.
General Douglas MacArthur had a risky plan. Land troops on the west coast, at Inchon, far behind the North Korean army.
Inchon was a terrible place for a landing. It has some of the biggest tides in the world, up to about 30 feet. Ships could only get in at high tide, and only for a few hours.
Many officers thought it would fail. But on September 15, 1950, Marines hit the beach, and the North Koreans were caught almost completely by surprise.
It worked. Within two weeks, American and South Korean troops took Seoul back. At the same time, the army in the Pusan corner broke out and charged north.
In a few weeks, the North Korean army went from winning the war to falling apart. Many of its soldiers were cut off behind the lines.
On October 1, South Korean troops crossed the 38th parallel going north. The goal was no longer to push North Korea back. It was to finish it.
On October 15, Truman flew to Wake Island to meet MacArthur. He asked whether China might join the war. MacArthur said the chance was very small.
Pyongyang fell on October 19. UN troops raced north toward the Yalu River, the border with China. Some of them got there.
In late November, MacArthur announced a final push, and reporters said it might end the war by Christmas. His intelligence officers kept saying China wouldn't send a big army.
But China had already sent its army. Starting on October 19, Chinese soldiers crossed the Yalu by night. In the mountains, they hid by day and marched at dusk.
On November 25, they hit the Americans and South Koreans with a huge surprise attack. In the west, the UN lines folded, and the whole army fell back.
In the east, about 30,000 Americans, British, and South Korean troops were cut off around the Chosin Reservoir. They were outnumbered about four to one, and it was as cold as 30 below zero.
The Marines fought their way out, about 80 miles to the sea, through snow and roadblocks. They came out carrying their wounded.
In December, ships took about 100,000 soldiers and nearly 100,000 Korean refugees out of Hungnam. One cargo ship, the Meredith Victory, carried about 14,000 people in one trip.
On New Year's Eve, the Chinese struck again. Seoul fell for the second time on January 4, 1951, and the UN army was pushed back below it.
A new commander had just arrived, General Matthew Ridgway. He didn't want to hold ground at any price. He told his troops to hit the enemy hard and keep the army together.
By March, the UN army was moving north again. Seoul changed hands for the fourth time on March 15, 1951. In nine months, the capital had been captured four times.
In April, Truman fired MacArthur. The general had been arguing in public with the president about how far to take the war, and Truman decided only one of them could be in charge.
MacArthur came home to big parades and a speech to Congress. But Truman's advisers stuck to the plan: keep the war limited, and don't start World War Three.
By summer, the front had settled near the 38th parallel. Both sides were tired, and neither could win cheaply. So they agreed to talk.
The talks started on July 10, 1951, in Kaesong, and later moved to a truce village at Panmunjom. Many expected a deal in a few weeks. It took two years.
Why so long? Mostly one issue. Many prisoners did not want to go home, and the communist side said they had to. The UN side refused to force them.
Meanwhile, soldiers kept dying over hills with names like Heartbreak Ridge and Pork Chop Hill. Men fought for months over land that barely moved on the map.
Both sides dug in with trenches and bunkers. It started to look like World War One, with jets fighting overhead.
The deal finally came on July 27, 1953. It was a ceasefire, signed in a hastily built hall at Panmunjom. No peace treaty. Just an agreement to stop shooting.
The new line followed the front where the armies stood. It ran a little north of the old line in the east, and a little south of it in the west. Almost exactly where it started.
That border is still there. It's called the DMZ, the Demilitarized Zone, about 150 miles long and 2.5 miles wide. It's one of the most heavily armed borders on Earth.
Remember the pencil line from the start? After three years and millions of lives, the border ended up almost in the same place. The only thing that changed was the cost.

More than 36,000 Americans died in Korea. That's about as many people as fill Fenway Park on a sold-out night. South Korea lost more than 130,000 soldiers, and the estimates for China and North Korea are higher, though they're disputed.

beats.say: Millions of Korean civilians died too. Estimates run from about one and a half million to three million, and nobody knows the exact number.
So who won? Nobody, really. South Korea survived and grew rich. North Korea stayed under one family for three generations. And the two Koreas are still technically at war.
The line a few officers drew in thirty minutes still splits a country of more than 75 million people. Was there a moment this could have stopped sooner? Tell me which one in the comments.
